name: B. R. Ambedkar
info: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar (1891–1956) was an Indian jurist, economist, social reformer and politician, born into a Mahar family treated as untouchable, who chaired the committee that drafted the Constitution of India and led mass conversions to Buddhism.

facts.born: 14 April 1891 in the town and military cantonment of Mhow (now Dr Ambedkar Nagar, Madhya Pradesh); the 14th and last child of Ramji Maloji Sakpal, a subedar in the British Indian Army, and Bhimabai Sakpal, of a Marathi Mahar family from Ambadawe in Ratnagiri district
facts.died: 6 December 1956 at his home in Delhi, in his sleep, three days after finishing his manuscript The Buddha and His Dhamma; cremated in a Buddhist ceremony at Dadar Chowpatty beach on 7 December
facts.role: Professor of political economy at Sydenham College (from 1918); principal of the Government Law College, Bombay (1935, for two years); founder of the Independent Labour Party (1936) and the Scheduled Castes Federation; minister of labour on the Viceroy's Executive Council; Law Minister in Nehru's first cabinet (1947 to 1951); chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution; member of the Rajya Sabha
facts.known: campaigns against untouchability, including the Mahad satyagraha of 1927; the Poona Pact of 1932; Annihilation of Caste (1936); chairing the drafting of the Constitution of India; writings on economics, including The Problem of the Rupee; his conversion to Buddhism in 1956 and the mass conversions that followed

t: Born a Mahar, a caste treated as untouchable, Ambedkar was segregated at school, yet went on to doctorates at Columbia University and the London School of Economics and was called to the Bar at Gray's Inn.

From 1927 he led marches, water and temple campaigns and the burning of the Manusmriti against untouchability, and in 1932 he signed the Poona Pact with Madan Mohan Malaviya after Gandhi's fast against separate electorates.

He chaired the drafting of the Constitution of India, resigned from Nehru's cabinet in 1951 when the Hindu code bill was defeated, and in 1956 converted to Buddhism at Nagpur with some 500,000 followers.
dyk: At school Ambedkar had to sit on a gunny sack that he took home with him, and when he needed water someone had to pour it for him from a height, which he later summed up as "No peon, No Water". His personal library held more than 50,000 books.
ev: Born at Mhow, the 14th child of Ramji Maloji Sakpal, into a Mahar family
Awarded a Baroda State Scholarship to study at Columbia University in New York City
Begins active movements against untouchability, leading the Mahad satyagraha for the right to draw water from the town's main tank and, in December, burning copies of the Manusmriti
Signs the Poona Pact with Madan Mohan Malaviya, giving the Depressed Classes reserved seats within the general electorate
Publishes Annihilation of Caste and founds the Independent Labour Party
Becomes Law Minister in Nehru's cabinet and is appointed Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution
Converts to Buddhism at Nagpur and then converts some 500,000 of his supporters
Dies in his sleep at his home in Delhi on 6 December

sections.early:
Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was born on 14 April 1891 at Mhow, a town and military cantonment now officially called Dr Ambedkar Nagar, in Madhya Pradesh. He was the 14th and last child of Ramji Maloji Sakpal, a subedar in the British Indian Army, and Bhimabai Sakpal. The family came from Ambadawe in Ratnagiri district and belonged to the Mahar caste, which was treated as untouchable and subjected to socio-economic discrimination. At school he and other untouchable children were segregated, were not allowed to sit inside the class and were given little help by teachers.

His father retired in 1894 and the family moved to Satara two years later; soon afterwards his mother died, and a paternal aunt cared for the children in difficult circumstances. Of his brothers and sisters only Ambedkar passed his examinations and went to high school. His surname in the records changed from Sakpal to Ambadawekar and then to Ambedkar, the name of a Brahmin teacher, Krishnaji Keshav Ambedkar.

In 1897 the family moved to Mumbai, where he was the only untouchable enrolled at Elphinstone High School. In 1906 he married Ramabai in a match arranged by their parents. He passed his matriculation in 1907 and entered Elphinstone College, becoming, by his own account, the first from his caste to do so, and by 1912 he held a degree in economics and political science from Bombay University.
sections.rise:
In 1913, a few weeks after his father's death, Ambedkar was awarded a Baroda State Scholarship under a scheme of Sayajirao Gaekwad III, the Gaekwad of Baroda, for postgraduate study at Columbia University in New York City. He passed his M.A. in June 1915, majoring in economics, and was influenced there by John Dewey. In 1916 he presented the paper Castes in India: Their Mechanism, Genesis and Development to a seminar run by the anthropologist Alexander Goldenweiser, and in October of that year he enrolled at Gray's Inn and at the London School of Economics.

He returned to India in 1917 when his scholarship ended, and went back to London in 1920 with support from Shahu of Kolhapur. He completed a master of science degree at the LSE in 1921, and in 1923 the University of London awarded him a D.Sc. in economics for The Problem of the Rupee; the same year he was called to the Bar. His Columbia Ph.D. followed in 1927.

Back in India he struggled to make a living: an investment consulting business failed when clients learned he was an untouchable. In 1918 he became professor of political economy at Sydenham College, where other professors objected to his sharing a drinking-water jug with students. In 1920 he began the weekly Mooknayak with Shahu's help, and he later founded the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha to promote education and welfare among the "outcastes".
sections.deeds:
By 1927 Ambedkar had decided to launch active movements against untouchability. He led a satyagraha at Mahad for the right of untouchables to draw water from the town's main water tank. At a conference in late 1927 he condemned the Manusmriti for justifying caste discrimination, and on 25 December he led thousands of followers in burning copies of it. In 1930 he launched the Kalaram Temple movement at Nashik, in which about 15,000 volunteers marched to the temple gates, which Brahmin authorities closed.

In 1932 the British government's Communal Award announced a separate electorate for the "Depressed Classes". Gandhi, who feared it would divide the Hindu community, fasted in Yerwada jail. The Poona Pact of 24 September 1932, signed by Ambedkar and Madan Mohan Malaviya among 23 signatories, gave reserved seats within the general electorate, 148 in the provincial legislatures instead of the 71 of the Communal Award.

Ambedkar published Annihilation of Caste on 15 May 1936 and founded the Independent Labour Party, which won 11 of the 13 reserved and 3 of the 4 general seats it contested in 1937. He tabled a bill against the khoti system in Konkan and served on the Viceroy's Executive Council as minister of labour. After independence he became Law Minister and chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution, which was adopted on 26 November 1949 and included reservations in civil services, schools and colleges for scheduled castes and tribes.
sections.opponents:
Ambedkar's opponents included orthodox Hindu leaders, whom Annihilation of Caste strongly criticised, and Gandhi, whom the book rebuked. Gandhi fiercely opposed a separate electorate for untouchables, and in a 1955 BBC interview Ambedkar accused him of writing against the caste system in English-language papers while supporting it in Gujarati ones. He also accused Nehru of being "conscious of the fact that he is a Brahmin". His claim that Hinduism was the foundation of the caste system made him controversial and unpopular among Hindus.

He was no ally of the Communists, of whom he said in 1938: "I am an implacable enemy of the Communists." The Marxist theorist Abhinav Sinha replied that Ambedkar had not read Marx, Engels or Lenin. In Pakistan or The Partition of India (1940) he argued that attempts to forge Hindu-Muslim unity within one state would lead to continuous conflict, and he accepted that Punjab and Bengal should be redrawn with compulsory population exchanges. He also criticised child marriage and the treatment of women in Muslim society.

Critics have faulted him for one-sided views on caste at the expense of cooperation with the larger nationalist movement, and some biographers for neglecting organisation-building. In 1953 he told parliament that he had been a "hack" on the constitution, that he had acted "much against my will" and that he would be "the first person to burn it out". His Riddles in Hinduism, published after his death, led to mass demonstrations and counter-demonstrations.
sections.last:
Ramabai died in 1935 after a long illness. At the Yeola Conversion Conference on 13 October that year Ambedkar announced his intention to convert to another religion, and he said that he had been born a Hindu but would not die one. He considered Sikhism but concluded that he might get "second-rate" status there. Around 1950 he turned to Buddhism, travelled to Ceylon for a meeting of the World Fellowship of Buddhists and visited Burma twice in 1954. He founded the Bharatiya Bauddha Mahasabha in 1955.

On 27 September 1951 he resigned from Nehru's cabinet after the Hindu code bill was defeated. He lost the 1952 election in Bombay North to his former assistant Narayan Sadoba Kajrolkar, and placed third in the 1954 by-election at Bhandara. He married Sharada Kabir, a doctor, on 15 April 1948, and she took the name Savita Ambedkar. He had diabetes from 1948 and spent June to October 1954 in bed.

In Nagpur on 14 October 1956 he accepted the Three Refuges and Five Precepts from a Buddhist monk and then converted some 500,000 of his supporters, for whom he prescribed 22 Vows. He died in his sleep in Delhi on 6 December 1956, three days after completing The Buddha and His Dhamma. Half a million people attended his cremation at Dadar Chowpatty beach, and no ministers attended. Further conversions took place there on 16 December.
sections.legacy:
Ambedkar's political philosophy has given rise to many political parties, publications and workers' unions across India, especially in Maharashtra. His conversion renewed interest in Buddhist philosophy in India and abroad, and later mass conversion ceremonies have followed the Nagpur example of 1956. Some Indian Buddhists regard him as a Bodhisattva, which he never claimed himself. In the late 1990s some Hungarian Romani people, inspired by him, began to convert to Buddhism. The Bharatiya Bauddha Mahasabha he founded was led after him by his son Yashwant Ambedkar.

His birthday, Ambedkar Jayanti, is a public holiday in many Indian states, and he received the Bharat Ratna posthumously in 1990. His bronze statue was installed in the Parliament of India in 1967. Scholar Anand Teltumbde noted that in the Congress's years of monopoly he was neglected, and that ten years after his death there was no road or monument in his name. Steven Calabresi, agreeing with Martha Nussbaum, has called the constitution "Ambedkar's constitution" for the purposive approach the Supreme Court later took, which Ambedkar had supported in a minority.

The economist Amartya Sen has called him the "father of my economics", and Narendra Jadhav described him as the highest educated Indian economist of all times. Ambedkar himself, in his concluding speech of 25 November 1949, said the credit for the constitution belonged partly to Sir B. N. Rau, who prepared its rough draft. His salutation "Jai Bhim" and the title Babasaheb are used by his followers.

summary: B. R. Ambedkar (1891–1956), born into a Mahar family treated as untouchable, studied at Columbia and the London School of Economics and led campaigns against untouchability. He chaired the drafting of the Constitution of India and in 1956 converted to Buddhism with some 500,000 followers.

Aishwary Kumar, Radical Equality: Ambedkar, Gandhi, and the Risk of Democracy (Stanford University Press, 2015)
Gail Omvedt, Ambedkar: Towards an Enlightened India (Penguin, 2004)
Shashi Tharoor, B. R. Ambedkar: The Man Who Gave Hope to India's Dispossessed (Manchester University Press, 2023)
notes: Conversion date: the Conversion section and Wikipedia's account give 14 October 1956 at Nagpur; the Views section says 16 October 1956. The text follows 14 October (also the Dhamma Chakra Pravartan Din date given in Death).

Doctorates: the lead says doctorates in 1927 (Columbia) and 1923 (LSE); the Education section calls the LSE degree a D.Sc. from the University of London in 1923. The text says D.Sc. from the University of London, which is how the Education section puts it.

The Economics section calls The Evolution of Provincial Finance his PhD dissertation, while Education says the LSE doctoral thesis was The Problem of the Rupee; the Columbia Ph.D. title is not stated in Education. The text names only The Problem of the Rupee, with the D.Sc.
Rajya Sabha: the article says 'probably an appointed member'; the facts say 'member of the Rajya Sabha' without the hedge about appointment. Dates of membership are not given.

He was Law Minister in Nehru's first cabinet and resigned 27 September 1951; the role fact gives 1947 to 1951 from those two statements. The article says he was appointed Chairman of the Drafting Committee two weeks after independence.

Law College principal 'for two years' from 1935 is the article's wording. The 'about 15,000 volunteers' at Kalaram is the article's figure; 'one of the greatest processions of Nashik' was left out as the article's own praise.
Poona Pact seats: 148 in 'Provisional legislatures' (the article's word; read as provincial) against 71 in the Communal Award; the Pact's text is left as the article has it.

Left out: the poll naming him 'the Greatest Indian', film and television portrayals, the Google doodle, statues of 2023 to 2026, the Ambedkar family list, the Works bibliography, the Austrian-school and state-socialism economics sections beyond the rupee thesis, his views on Jews, the Aryan question and Christianity, and the Day of Deliverance passage (both Jinnah and he were quoted at length).

The section 'last' and 'legacy' mix some chronology (cabinet resignation after conversion plans) because the article does not date the Sikh consideration; the text keeps the article's order of topics.
Ambedkar's year of birth 1891 and death 1956 are firm in the article; no circa.
